description: Persistent memory for the roles that review the same codebase repeatedly. A reviewer that has read this repository forty times knows things a fresh one does not, and re-deriving them every session is the cost this removes. What it must never become is a second source of truth.

the_rule.means: It can make a role faster at finding something, and it can never make a role right about something. Where memory and durable state disagree, durable state wins and the memory is wrong.
authority_remains: approved artifacts — what was decided and reviewed
the work item and the task graph — what is being done and by whom
decision records — why, and who decided
the_rule.consequence: A finding whose only support is a memory is not a finding. It is a reason to go and look at the artifact, and the artifact is what the finding cites.

what_it_is_for: Recurring codebase patterns: where a thing lives, what a convention is, which module is the one everybody gets wrong.
Recurring review findings: the mistake this codebase keeps making, so the reviewer looks for it early rather than finding it on the fourth pass.
Project-specific architectural observations: which boundaries are real and which are nominal, what the actual coupling is as opposed to the declared coupling.
Debugging insights: what a symptom turned out to mean last time, and where the investigation started paying off.
what_it_is_not_for: Verdicts. A previous approval is not evidence about this change, and remembering that something passed is how a reviewer stops reviewing.
Policy. What is required lives in policies/ and changes without telling the memory.
Approvals. A remembered human decision is a decision nobody can audit, and an agent verdict was never an approval to begin with.
Requirements, targets or numbers. A remembered NFR is a number with no owner.
Anything about a person. Not who writes bad code, not who is slow to review.
Anything the artifact already says. Memory that duplicates durable state is a copy that goes stale silently.

how_to_write_one.why_this_matters: Memory does not only record. Verified live against 2.1.250: given the bare fact 'the retention window is 30 days', the agent wrote back an invented justification -- 'likely driven by compliance standards, regulatory frameworks, or internal data governance policies' -- and promoted the fact into a rule it would enforce: 'Flag any architectural decisions or cleanup operations that might violate this window.' Nobody said either of those things. Left alone, memory manufactures a `why` and an imperative, and the next session applies both as though they were policy.
rules: Record the observation and where it was observed. `docs/architecture/ACME-ARCH-004 says the transfer path is synchronous` is a memory. `the transfer path is synchronous` is a claim with no owner.
Never record a justification you were not given. If nobody said why, the memory says what and stops.
Never write a memory in the imperative. `Flag any change that...` is a rule; a role that writes rules for itself has replaced the policy with its own recollection.
Date it, or name the artifact version it came from. A memory with no age cannot be recognised as stale.
Prefer a pointer to a copy. `the retry policy is in ACME-ARCH-002 section 4` survives the retry policy changing; the retry policy itself does not.

scope.why: The CLI's own guidance says project scope is 'shared with your team via version control' and stores it at <project>/.claude/agent-memory/<agent>/. That makes it reviewable in a diff like every other artifact, which is the only reason it is safe to give a reviewer memory at all.
scope.user_is_forbidden: User scope stores at ~/.claude/agent-memory and applies across every project. A reviewer carrying an observation from one client's codebase into another's is a reasoning error and a confidentiality incident, and which one it is depends on facts the plugin cannot see.
scope.local_is_forbidden: Local scope is explicitly not checked into version control. A memory nobody can review is a private model of the codebase held by an agent, which is the thing this policy exists to prevent.
scope.enforced_by: scripts/validate_plugin.py refuses any agent declaring a scope other than project.

roles.why: Reviews the same structure repeatedly. What the real boundaries are, as opposed to the declared ones, is expensive to re-derive and cheap to remember.
Sees every diff. The mistake this codebase keeps making is the highest-value thing a reviewer can know before it starts reading.
A baseline is only meaningful against history, and the hot paths of a system are learned rather than declared.
What has actually failed here, and how, is the input to every review it does.
Evaluates this organization's own agents across releases, and the pattern in what agents get wrong is the substance of that job.

who_holds_it.why_only_reviewers: These five read the same repository repeatedly and produce findings rather than artifacts. A role that authors gets no memory: an author with recollections of what it decided last time will reproduce them, which is how a codebase acquires a convention nobody chose.
who_holds_it.adding_one: A governance decision under AP-10, recorded here with the reason. The list is not a default that grew.

not_enforceable: No hook sees a memory write. The platform writes it, not the Write tool, so guard_write never fires and the write scope in policies/write-scope.json does not apply. What makes project-scope memory reviewable is that it lands in the repository and a human reads the diff.

Nothing stops a role treating a memory as authority in its reasoning. The instruction is a contract like every other role instruction, and the compensating control is that a finding must cite an artifact -- a finding whose only support is a recollection has nothing to cite.
Nothing detects a stale memory. An artifact changes and the memory that described it does not; the pointer-over-copy rule reduces this and does not remove it.
Memory is written by the same model whose reasoning it will later shape. Nothing external validates an entry before it is stored.

review.cadence: A memory directory is reviewed when the role that owns it is reviewed, per policies/agent-lifecycle.json.
what_to_look_for: An entry written as a rule rather than an observation.
An entry carrying a justification nobody gave.
An entry that duplicates something an artifact says.
An entry old enough that the thing it describes has probably changed.
review.deleting_one: Deleting a memory needs no approval. It is a cache, and the cost of dropping a true one is that it gets re-derived.

lint.description: Deterministic checks over committed project-scope memory. A repository check, never a runtime one: the platform writes memory, not the Write tool, so no hook can intercept an entry as it is created. What can be done is read what landed in the repository, which is the whole reason project scope is the only permitted scope.
lint.what_it_can_decide: Shape. Whether an entry names where it came from and when, and whether it is written as an observation rather than as a rule. It cannot decide whether an observation is true, or useful, or worth keeping -- those are read by a person during the role's review.

rules.means: The entry names the artifact, file, path or run it was observed in.
rules.why: `the transfer path is synchronous` is a claim with no owner. `ACME-ARCH-004 says the transfer path is synchronous` can be checked, and can be found to have gone stale.

rules.means: The entry carries a date, or the version of the artifact it describes.
rules.why: A memory with no age cannot be recognised as stale, and staleness is the failure mode this kind of store has.

rules.means: No speculative `why` -- likely, probably, presumably, this suggests, driven by.
rules.why: The behaviour that was observed live: told the retention window is 30 days, the agent wrote back 'likely driven by compliance standards, regulatory frameworks, or internal data governance policies'. Nobody said that.

rules.means: No imperative or policy language -- must, shall, always, never, ensure that, flag any, do not.
rules.why: The other half of the same observation: it promoted the fact to 'Flag any architectural decisions or cleanup operations that might violate this window.' A role that writes rules for itself has replaced the policy with its own recollection.

rules.means: No stored requirement, NFR, SLO, threshold or quantified target.
rules.why: A remembered target is a number with no owner. Targets live in approved artifacts, which change without telling the memory.

rules.means: No stored review verdict, approval, sign-off or AP- reference.
rules.why: A remembered approval is a decision nobody can audit, and an agent verdict was never an approval to begin with. Remembering that something passed is how a reviewer stops reviewing.

rules.means: No named individual, handle or email.
rules.why: Not who writes bad code, not who is slow to review. An agent accumulating observations about people is a different product with a different set of obligations.

rules.means: Every artifact id the entry names exists in the project.
rules.why: A pointer to something that has been superseded or deleted is worse than no pointer: it reads as provenance and leads nowhere.

rules.means: Every entry file is listed in MEMORY.md, and every MEMORY.md line resolves.
rules.why: The index is what a reviewer reads. An entry outside it is a memory nobody reviewed.

lint.severity: ML-03, ML-04, ML-05, ML-06 and ML-07 are errors: each is the memory becoming something it is not permitted to be. ML-01, ML-02, ML-08 and ML-09 are warnings, because an entry that is merely under-sourced is repairable and a lint that blocks a build over provenance teaches people to delete memories rather than fix them.
not_enforceable: Whether an observation is true. The lint reads shape, and a well-formed entry can be entirely wrong.
Whether an entry duplicates what an artifact already says. It can see that an artifact is named; it cannot compare the claim against the artifact's current content.
Anything about memory that was never committed. Local-scope memory is invisible to this by construction, which is one of the reasons local scope is forbidden here.
